identity.title: Temporal superposition and feature geometry of RNNs under memory demands

problem.claim: How memory demands shape representational geometry and strategies in recurrent neural networks.

gap.claim: The effect of time or memory as a capacity constraint on recurrent-model representational geometry is not well understood.

contributions.claim: Introduces temporal superposition for analyzing memory-dependent representations in RNNs.

Develops a theoretical framework for linear-recurrence RNNs on delayed serial recall, relating data properties, task demands, and dimensionality to representational strategies, with stated generalization to nonlinear RNNs.
Analyzes the interaction between spatial and temporal superposition and the resulting representational tradeoffs.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors present temporal superposition as a concept for understanding memory effects on recurrent representations.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report an effectively linear, dense regime and a sparse regime using an interference-free space.
They report that the regimes are characterized by a phase transition in feature angular distributions and a decrease in spectral radius.
They report that insights from the linear-recurrence framework generalize to nonlinear RNNs.

narrative_sequence.summary: Distributed representations can compress more features than neurons through non-orthogonal superposition.
The role of time or memory as an additional capacity constraint in recurrent representational geometry remains unclear.
The work studies memory effects via temporal superposition and a linear-recurrence delayed-serial-recall framework.
The analysis identifies dense and sparse regimes, associated geometric and spectral changes, and interactions between spatial and temporal superposition.
The authors frame these results as a mechanistic geometric explanation of how capacity and task demands shape learned RNN strategies.

source_observation.claim: The abstract links representational regimes to task demands, capacity, feature-angle distributions, and spectral radius.

lessons.interpretation: A mechanism-focused account can connect abstract representational geometry to measurable regime indicators and task conditions.
lessons.application: When presenting a representation-learning result, map each proposed strategy to task pressure, capacity, and observable geometric or dynamical signatures.
lessons.exception: This framing may be unsuitable when the work lacks interpretable geometric or dynamical diagnostics.

unknowns: The abstract does not provide quantitative regime boundaries, phase-transition conditions, or spectral-radius values.
The evidence and claimed generalization to nonlinear RNNs are not accompanied by experimental setup, baselines, sample sizes, or detailed evaluation results.
The abstract does not specify how spatial and temporal tradeoffs are measured.
